# Chapter 3: Methods

## Survey Data

### Population

The target population for the survey will consist of current CVRx commercial field employees who are expected to use Salesforce as part of their regular job responsibilities. This includes territory managers and other approved field roles whose work involves managing accounts and opportunities, documenting customer interactions, or completing Salesforce workflows.

Area sales directors may also be included. Because the core questionnaire items are written for individual contributors, a short manager-focused version is proposed for area sales directors, pending faculty-lead and CVRx approval.

Employees who do not use Salesforce in a field role are outside the target population and will be screened out through the first survey question (Q1).

### Sampling Frame

The sampling frame will be CVRx's list of active commercial field employees with Salesforce access as of the survey distribution date. CVRx will maintain this list and distribute the survey internally, so the research team will not receive employee names or contact information.

Where CVRx approves it, the same de-identified user identifiers used in the Salesforce exports will be attached to survey invitations so that responses can be linked to AO1 adoption measures and AO3 segments. Employees who have left CVRx or moved out of a field role before distribution will be excluded. The size of the frame will be confirmed by CVRx.

\[Open item: number of eligible field users in the frame.\]

### Sampling Method

The survey will use a census approach. Every employee in the sampling frame will be invited to participate rather than a randomly selected subset. This approach is appropriate because CVRx's commercial field organization is relatively small, and a census maximizes the number of responses available for analysis.

Participation will be voluntary, so the final set of respondents will be self-selected, which is a non-probability sample. To assess possible non-response bias, the distribution of respondents by role, region and tenure will be compared with the distribution in the sampling frame provided by CVRx. Respondents who answer "No" to the screening question (Q1) will be excluded from analysis.

For the AO4 pre/post survey, respondents will be classified as members of the intervention or comparison group according to the pilot design approved by CVRx.

### Data Collection

The survey will be administered online through Qualtrics as a self-administered questionnaire. The instrument was developed from the team's Construct and Measurement table and takes approximately 8 to 10 minutes to complete. It opens with an informed-consent statement that explains the purpose of the study, voluntary participation, the right to skip any question and how responses will be kept confidential.

The questionnaire is organized into the following sections:

- **Screening (Q1):** current use of Salesforce in a field role.
- **Adoption constructs (Q2–Q24):** perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, workflow compatibility, manager support, training effectiveness, trust in Salesforce data and administrative burden, measured on five-point Likert scales.
- **Barriers (Q25):** reasons records are not kept current (check all that apply).
- **Overall perception (Q26):** satisfaction with Salesforce, repeated after the pilot.
- **Pilot feedback (Q27–Q29):** intervention group only, after the pilot.
- **Usage behavior (B1–B4):** update frequency, update timing, primary device and weekly hours in Salesforce.
- **Background (C1–C7):** role, tenure, medical device sales experience, prior CRM experience, region, comfort with new technology and age group.
- **Open-ended items (O1–O2):** suggested improvements and other feedback.

Before launch, the instrument will be pretested with the faculty lead and two or three CVRx reviewers to check wording, length and fit with field roles. CVRx will distribute the survey link through an internal channel, accompanied by a note from commercial leadership encouraging participation. The baseline survey is planned for Spring 2027 after CVRx approves the final instrument, and the follow-up survey for AO4 will be administered after the pilot ends in Summer 2027.

\[Open items: fielding window and reminder schedule; whether the CPP Qualtrics account is approved by CVRx or a CVRx platform is required.\]

### Sample Characteristics

#### Age

Age will be measured by age group (C7: under 30, 30 to 39, 40 to 49, 50 or older). Frequencies and percentages will be reported. "Prefer not to say" responses will be treated as missing.

#### Gender

Gender will not be collected. Because CVRx's field organization is small, combining gender with role, region and tenure could make individual respondents identifiable. Gender is also not part of the research questions or hypotheses.

#### Race/Ethnicity

Race and ethnicity will not be collected, for the same confidentiality reason as gender. These variables are not part of the analytics objectives.

#### Education

Formal education will not be collected. Professional experience is more relevant to Salesforce adoption, and it will be captured through medical device sales experience (C3) and prior CRM experience (C4).

#### Income

Income will not be collected. Compensation is confidential to CVRx and is not relevant to the research questions. Asking about it could also reduce willingness to participate.

#### Occupation

All respondents will be CVRx commercial field employees. Occupation will be described through the following variables:

- Job role (C1).
- Tenure at CVRx (C2), recoded into newer (18 months or less) and tenured (more than 18 months).
- Region (C5).
- Total medical device sales experience (C3).
- Prior Salesforce or CRM experience (C4).

The respondent distribution on these variables will be compared with the sampling frame.

#### Relevant Behavioral Variables

Relevant self-reported behaviors will include:

- How often the respondent updates Salesforce records in a typical week (B1).
- When the respondent usually records a customer interaction (B2).
- Reasons records are not kept current (Q25).
- Comfort with learning new software tools (C6).

#### Product Usage Variables

Relevant Salesforce usage characteristics will include:

- Hours per week spent entering or updating Salesforce information (B4).
- Primary device used to update Salesforce (B3).
- Overall satisfaction with Salesforce (Q26).
- Pilot participation and pilot feedback (Q27–Q29), for AO4 respondents.

### Measures

#### Independent Variables

- **Perceived usefulness (Q2–Q5):** the degree to which a user believes Salesforce improves job performance. Adapted from Davis (1989).
- **Perceived ease of use (Q6–Q9):** the degree to which using Salesforce is free of effort. Adapted from Davis (1989).
- **Workflow compatibility (Q10–Q12):** the degree to which Salesforce fits how field users work. Adapted from Goodhue and Thompson (1995).
- **Manager support (Q13–Q15):** the degree to which the user's manager encourages and uses Salesforce. Adapted from Avlonitis and Panagopoulos (2005) and Venkatesh et al. (2003).
- **Training effectiveness (Q16–Q18):** the degree to which training and resources prepared the user. Adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003).
- **Trust in Salesforce data (Q19–Q21):** the degree to which the user believes Salesforce information is accurate and current. Adapted from DeLone and McLean (2003).
- **Administrative burden (Q22–Q24):** the degree to which Salesforce adds time-consuming or duplicate work. Developed by the team.
- **Measurement period and intervention-group status (AO4):** baseline versus follow-up, and intervention versus comparison group.

Each construct is measured on a five-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 5 = Strongly agree). Items will be averaged into a composite score when Cronbach's alpha is 0.70 or higher.

#### Dependent Variables

- **Meaningful Salesforce adoption (AO2):** the AO1 Salesforce Adoption Index for the survey period, if CVRx approves linking survey responses to Salesforce records.
- **Self-reported update frequency (B1) and overall satisfaction (Q26):** used as the AO2 outcomes if linkage is not approved.
- **Overall satisfaction (Q26) and construct scores at follow-up (AO4):** used to evaluate changes in perceptions after the pilot.
- **Pilot feedback (Q27–Q29):** evaluation of the intervention by pilot participants.

#### Control Variables

- Job role (C1).
- Tenure group (C2).
- Region (C5).
- Medical device sales experience (C3).
- Prior CRM experience (C4).
- Comfort with new technology (C6).
- Age group (C7).
- Primary device (B3).
- Hours per week in Salesforce (B4).

The number of controls in any model will be limited by the final sample size (see AO2).

### Analytics Methods to Employ

#### AO1 — Measure Meaningful Salesforce Adoption (Luis Berumen)

**Method**

Survey data will not be the main source used to calculate the Salesforce Adoption Index. AO1 will primarily measure adoption through approved Salesforce records because those records show whether required updates, fields, interactions, and workflow steps were completed. Survey responses may still be used to provide context for the behavioral results and to check whether employees' descriptions of their Salesforce use are consistent with the patterns found in the system data.

The survey analysis for AO1 will begin with descriptive statistics such as response counts, percentages, means, and response distributions. Questions related to self-reported Salesforce use, update habits, and workflow completion may be summarized for the overall sample and, when the sample size permits, compared across approved roles or groups.

If CVRx approves de-identified identifiers that can be used across both data sources, survey responses may be matched with the Salesforce Adoption Index for the same user and time period. The analysis may then compare self-reported use with the overall index and its separate components. If individual-level matching is not approved, the survey and Salesforce results will remain separate and will only be compared at an aggregate level.

**Justification**

This approach keeps AO1 focused on observed Salesforce behavior instead of relying only on what employees report about their own use. A user may believe that Salesforce is being used regularly even when required records are incomplete or updates are entered too late. At the same time, Salesforce records cannot show how users view the system or why a particular adoption pattern exists.

This distinction is supported by research showing that system usage should be measured in relation to the user, system, and task rather than through one general activity measure [@burtonjones2006]. The Information Systems Success Model also treats system use and information quality as related but separate parts of system success [@delone2003]. For AO1, the survey therefore provides supporting evidence, while the approved Salesforce records provide the primary behavioral measures.

Using the survey as a supporting source can help determine whether the behavioral baseline and users' descriptions of their own use show a similar pattern. The results may also help identify areas that should be examined more closely under AO2. AO1 will measure what the adoption pattern looks like, while AO2 will examine the barriers and drivers that may explain that pattern.

**Variables**

Survey variables relevant to AO1 may include self-reported frequency of Salesforce use, timeliness of updates, completion of required fields, documentation of customer interactions, and consistency with required workflows. Approved user characteristics such as role, territory, tenure, and training experience may be used to describe the survey sample or support fair group comparisons.

If data linkage is approved, the Salesforce Adoption Index and its five component scores may be included as behavioral comparison measures. The final variables and comparisons will depend on the approved survey questions, response rate, available Salesforce fields, and CVRx's data-sharing requirements.

Self-reported frequency and agreement questions will generally be treated as ordinal measures unless a question requests a numerical count. Role and territory will be nominal variables, while tenure may be measured as a ratio variable when it is recorded in months or years. The Salesforce Adoption Index will be treated as a continuous composite index from 0 to 100. For AO1, the index and its component scores are the outcome measures, while approved user characteristics are comparison or control variables. AO2 will use the perception and experience measures to examine possible adoption drivers and barriers.

#### AO2 — Identify Drivers and Barriers of Meaningful Salesforce Adoption (Mickyas Shawel)

**Method**

AO2 will use the survey to identify which perceptions and organizational conditions are associated with stronger or weaker Salesforce adoption. The analysis will follow five steps.

1.  **Reliability and scoring.** The internal consistency of each multi-item construct will be assessed with Cronbach's alpha. Constructs that meet the 0.70 threshold will be scored as the mean of their items. Constructs below the threshold will be examined at the item level.

2.  **Descriptive analysis.** Construct scores will be summarized with means, standard deviations and response distributions. Barrier frequencies from Q25 will be reported as percentages of respondents.

3.  **Group comparisons.** Construct scores will be compared across role, region and tenure group using independent-samples t-tests or one-way ANOVA. Mann-Whitney U or Kruskal-Wallis tests will be used if assumptions are not met.

4.  **Correlation and regression.** Pearson correlations will examine bivariate relationships between each construct and adoption. A multiple linear regression will then estimate the association between each construct and adoption while holding the others constant:

    $$
    \text{Adoption}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PU}_i + \beta_2 \text{PEOU}_i + \beta_3 \text{WF}_i + \beta_4 \text{MGR}_i + \beta_5 \text{TRAIN}_i + \beta_6 \text{TRUST}_i + \beta_7 \text{BURDEN}_i + \boldsymbol{\gamma}\mathbf{X}_i + \varepsilon_i
    $$

    H1 will be supported if the coefficient for perceived usefulness (β~1~) is positive and statistically significant. H2 will be supported if the coefficient for administrative burden (β~7~) is negative and statistically significant. Multicollinearity will be checked with variance inflation factors. A common guideline calls for roughly 10 to 15 responses per predictor. If the final sample is too small for the full model, the analysis will focus on the hypothesized constructs (perceived usefulness and administrative burden) with a limited set of controls, and the results will be reported as exploratory.

5.  **Qualitative analysis.** Open-ended responses (O1, O2) will be coded thematically to explain the quantitative results and identify barriers not captured by the closed-ended items.

The adoption outcome will depend on CVRx's data-sharing approval. If linkage is approved, the dependent variable will be each respondent's Salesforce Adoption Index from AO1. If linkage is not approved, self-reported update frequency (B1) and overall satisfaction (Q26) will serve as the dependent variables, and the analysis will be interpreted at the perception level.

**Justification**

The model is grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT; Venkatesh et al., 2003) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; Davis, 1989), which are among the most widely validated frameworks for explaining technology adoption in the workplace. Organizational constructs are added because sales technology research shows that adoption depends on manager support, workflow fit and data quality as well as individual attitudes (Avlonitis and Panagopoulos, 2005; Goodhue and Thompson, 1995; DeLone and McLean, 2003).

Salesforce records show what users do but not why. The survey measures the perceptions behind adoption behavior, and regression estimates the relative strength of each factor. This answers R3 and R4 and tests H1 and H2. The resulting drivers and barriers will be used to interpret AO3 segments and to select the behaviors targeted in the AO4 intervention.

**Variables**

- **Dependent:** the Salesforce Adoption Index (SF1) if linked; otherwise update frequency (B1) and overall satisfaction (Q26).
- **Independent:** perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, workflow compatibility, manager support, training effectiveness, trust in Salesforce data and administrative burden (Q2–Q24); barrier indicators (Q25).
- **Control:** role, tenure group, region, medical device sales experience, prior CRM experience, comfort with new technology, primary device and weekly hours in Salesforce.

#### AO3 — Salesforce User Segmentation and Targeted Engagement (Tim Arana)

**Method**

Survey data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and group comparisons to examine differences in Salesforce adoption perceptions, barriers, and engagement needs among CVRx commercial field users. The analysis will build on the adoption-related constructs examined in AO2, including perceived usefulness, ease of use, workflow compatibility, manager support, training effectiveness, trust in Salesforce data, and administrative burden.

Survey responses will first be summarized using frequencies, percentages, means, and measures of variation, as appropriate for each variable. These summaries will help identify common experiences and potential differences across respondents. Where sample size permits, comparisons may be conducted across relevant employee characteristics, such as job role, tenure, or territory.

If CVRx approves the use of consistent de-identified identifiers, survey responses may also be linked to Salesforce adoption measures developed under AO1 and the behavioral user segments identified through AO3. This would allow the analysis to examine whether users within different behavioral segments report different adoption barriers, perceptions, or support needs.

If individual-level linkage is not permitted, survey responses will be analyzed separately and interpreted at an aggregate level. The final analytical procedures will depend on survey participation, available variables, and CVRx's data-sharing approvals.

**Justification**

This approach supports AO3 by providing additional context for understanding differences in Salesforce adoption behavior. Although Salesforce records can reveal how frequently users complete required activities or maintain customer information, these records cannot directly explain employees' perceptions or experiences with the platform.

Survey analysis can help identify whether different user groups experience challenges related to training, administrative workload, managerial support, or perceived usefulness. For example, users with similar adoption patterns may report different reasons for using Salesforce consistently or inconsistently.

Examining these differences will help CVRx develop engagement recommendations that address the needs of specific user segments rather than applying identical communications or training to all employees.

The proposed approach is consistent with the hybrid behavioral and adoption-driver segmentation framework established in Chapter 2. Behavioral measures will provide the primary basis for identifying segments, while survey findings will help interpret those groups and determine which engagement strategies may be appropriate.

The resulting recommendations will also support AO4 by informing the selection of engagement tactics for the proposed intervention.

**Variables**

The primary survey variables will include perceived usefulness, ease of use, workflow compatibility, manager support, training effectiveness, trust in Salesforce data, and administrative burden. These constructs will be measured using relevant survey questions developed under AO2.

Additional variables may include employee role, tenure, territory, training experience, and other approved characteristics relevant to Salesforce adoption.

Where individual-level data linkage is approved, the Salesforce Adoption Index developed under AO1 and behavioral segment membership established under AO3 may be incorporated into group comparisons.

The final selection of variables will depend on the approved survey instrument, response rates, and the completeness and quality of the collected data.

#### AO4 — Implement and Evaluate an Engagement Campaign (Wenting Jiang)

**Method Used**

Survey responses collected before and after the targeted engagement intervention will be compared to evaluate changes in users’ Salesforce perceptions and experiences. Multi-item constructs will be created by averaging related five-point Likert-scale items. When the final sample size is sufficient, Cronbach’s alpha will be used to examine the internal consistency of each construct before a composite score is calculated.

The analysis will begin with descriptive statistics, including response counts, means, standard deviations and response distributions. If the same respondents can be confidentially matched across the two periods, paired-samples tests will be used. If individual responses cannot be matched, baseline and follow-up responses will be treated as independent samples. Nonparametric alternatives will be considered when the sample size or data distribution does not support a t-test.

If an intervention group and a credible comparison group are available, a difference-in-differences analysis will be considered. Open-ended responses will also be reviewed to identify recurring barriers, recommendations and user concerns.

**Justification for the Method**

A pre/post survey design is appropriate because AO4 examines whether the intervention changes users’ perceptions of Salesforce, the support they receive and their willingness to follow recommended Salesforce practices. Previous research indicates that technology adoption may be influenced by perceived usefulness, ease of use, training, managerial support and workflow compatibility.

Survey results will be interpreted together with Salesforce behavioral data because self-reported responses may be affected by recall error, social-desirability bias and common-method bias. Combining survey and behavioral data will provide a more complete evaluation of the intervention.

**Variables**

The primary survey outcomes will include perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, workflow compatibility, information quality, managerial support, training adequacy, administrative burden and overall satisfaction. Self-reported update frequency and timeliness may also be examined.

The main independent variables will be the measurement period, intervention-group status and, when applicable, the interaction between intervention-group status and the post-intervention period. Role, tenure, prior CRM experience, region and comfort with learning new software may be considered as contextual variables if the final sample size permits.

## Secondary Data

### Data Source

The secondary data for this project will consist of existing Salesforce CRM records maintained by CVRx as part of its commercial operations. These records may include account and opportunity information, customer interaction documentation, Salesforce activity history, workflow completion records, and relevant user characteristics such as role, team, territory, and tenure.

The research team will request access to approved, de-identified Salesforce exports containing the information necessary to evaluate meaningful adoption and user engagement. Potential data elements include opportunity update timeliness, record completeness, interaction documentation, workflow consistency, and platform activity. These measures will support the Salesforce Adoption Index developed under AO1 and the behavioral segmentation analysis proposed under AO3.

Data availability, historical coverage, and the specific Salesforce objects and fields included in the analysis will depend on CVRx's approval and data-sharing requirements. The team will analyze only authorized information within a CVRx-approved environment and report findings in aggregate to protect employee confidentiality.

### Population

The target population for the secondary data analysis will consist of CVRx commercial field employees who are expected to use Salesforce as part of their regular job responsibilities. This may include territory managers, area sales directors, and other approved commercial personnel whose responsibilities involve documenting customer interactions, managing opportunities, maintaining account information, or completing relevant Salesforce workflows.

The analysis will focus on employees whose Salesforce usage can be evaluated through the meaningful adoption measures developed under AO1. These measures may include record completeness, opportunity update timeliness, customer interaction documentation, workflow consistency, and platform activity.

The final population will depend on CVRx's confirmation of eligible employee roles, Salesforce access permissions, and available historical records. Users whose responsibilities do not require the same Salesforce activities may need to be evaluated separately to ensure that adoption comparisons are appropriate across different roles.

### Sampling Frame

The sampling frame for the secondary data analysis will consist of the approved Salesforce user records and associated CRM activity records provided by CVRx. The frame will include eligible commercial field employees whose Salesforce responsibilities and activities fall within the scope of the study.

Eligible records may include opportunity updates, account information, documented customer interactions, workflow completion history, and platform activity. Where available, de-identified user identifiers will be used to connect relevant Salesforce records across datasets and time periods without revealing individual employee identities.

The final sampling frame will depend on the completeness of the Salesforce exports, the historical period covered, and the user roles authorized by CVRx. Records with missing identifiers, insufficient activity history, or incompatible reporting periods will be evaluated before inclusion. Users with no eligible activity will not automatically be excluded, since inactivity may be relevant to measuring Salesforce adoption.

The research team will document any exclusions to ensure transparency and consistency in the analytical process.

### Sampling Method

The secondary data analysis will use a non-probability, purposive sampling approach based on the Salesforce records approved and provided by CVRx. The study will focus on commercial field employees whose job responsibilities require meaningful Salesforce usage and whose records fall within the authorized study period.

Where feasible, the research team will seek to include all eligible Salesforce users within the approved population, effectively conducting a census of the relevant field organization rather than selecting a smaller sample. This approach is appropriate because CVRx has a relatively limited commercial field organization, and including all eligible users would provide a more complete understanding of adoption patterns.

The final analytical sample will depend on the availability, completeness, and quality of the approved Salesforce records. Users will be evaluated according to consistent eligibility criteria, including their job responsibilities, relevant Salesforce workflows, and the availability of records during the study period.

The team will document any exclusions and assess whether differences in roles, territories, workloads, or employment tenure may affect comparisons between users. The sampling approach will prioritize comprehensive coverage of the eligible population while maintaining employee confidentiality through de-identified records and aggregate reporting.

### Data Wrangling

#### Import

Authorized Salesforce data will be obtained from CVRx after the required approvals are received. Depending on availability, the data may include user activity, opportunity records, customer-interaction records, workflow activities, modification dates and intervention-participation records. The exact datasets and fields will be determined after CVRx confirms the approved data scope. The original files will be maintained as read-only source files, and all cleaning and transformation procedures will be performed on working copies. Personal identifiers will be removed or replaced with anonymous study identifiers before analysis.

#### Tidying

The data will be examined for duplicate records, missing values, inconsistent categories, invalid dates and possible outliers. Date formats, role classifications, regions and record statuses will be standardized when necessary. Missing information will be distinguished from fields that are not required or applicable to a particular user, role or workflow. For example, a user will not receive a lower completeness score for a field that was not required for the relevant record. All cleaning and exclusion decisions will be documented.

#### Joining the Data

If multiple Salesforce datasets are provided, they will be joined using approved anonymous user IDs, record IDs and relevant dates. Potential datasets may include user information, opportunity records, customer interactions, workflow records and intervention-exposure records. Before and after each join, record counts will be checked to prevent the accidental duplication or loss of observations. Intervention records will only be linked to individual Salesforce outcomes when such linkage is authorized.

### Understanding the Data

#### Transform

After cleaning, Salesforce records will be summarized at an appropriate level, such as one observation per user per week or month. The final analytical unit will depend on the frequency and completeness of the available data. Planned transformations include calculating record completeness, update timeliness, workflow adherence, customer-interaction documentation and platform activity. Observations will also be classified into baseline, intervention and follow-up periods. Where appropriate, measures will be adjusted for eligible work volume so that users with different workloads can be compared more fairly. If the available fields support a composite meaningful-adoption score, the research team may combine several behavioral and data-quality measures. However, each component will also be reported separately to avoid hiding specific Salesforce adoption problems.

#### Visualize

Exploratory visualizations will be used to examine missing data, variable distributions, outliers and changes over time. Planned visualizations include histograms, box plots, trend charts and group-comparison charts. If intervention and comparison groups are available, their baseline and follow-up patterns will be plotted separately. Pre-intervention trends will also be examined when multiple baseline periods are available. These visualizations will support data understanding and model selection but will not be treated as sufficient evidence of causation.

### Programming

Data cleaning and analysis will be conducted in a reproducible statistical programming environment. Python or R will be used for data preparation, variable construction, statistical analysis and visualization. SQL may also be used if the Salesforce data require database extraction or aggregation. The final software, versions and packages will be documented after the analysis environment is confirmed. Raw data, cleaned data, analytical datasets, code and generated outputs will be stored separately. The code will document the treatment of missing data, eligibility rules, variable definitions and exclusions. Quality checks will include duplicate detection, verification of date ranges and comparisons of record counts before and after data joins. Relevant programming code and technical documentation will be included in the report appendix or approved team storage.

### Sample Characteristics

#### Relevant Demographic Variables

Relevant user characteristics may include:

- User role;
- Region or territory;
- Tenure at CVRx;
- Prior Salesforce or CRM experience; and
- Intervention or comparison-group membership.

#### Relevant Behavioral Variables

Relevant Salesforce-related behaviors may include:

- Number of opportunities;
- Number of customer interactions;
- Frequency of record updates;
- Timeliness of record updates;
- Record completeness;
- Customer-interaction documentation; and
- Completion of required workflow steps.

#### Product Usage Variables

Relevant Salesforce usage characteristics may include:

- Salesforce activity frequency;
- Number of records created or updated;
- Use of relevant Salesforce features;
- Frequency of documenting customer interactions;
- Use of required Salesforce workflows; and
- Participation in intervention-related activities, if available.

### Measures

#### Independent Variables

- **Intervention-group status:** Indicates whether a user belongs to the intervention or comparison group.
- **Post-intervention period:** Distinguishes follow-up observations from baseline observations.
- **Intervention × Post:** Measures whether the intervention group experienced a greater change than the comparison group.
- **Intervention exposure:** May include receipt of intervention materials, training attendance, or participation in intervention activities.

#### Dependent Variables

- **Record completeness:** Percentage of applicable required Salesforce fields containing valid information.
- **Update timeliness:** Time between an eligible activity and its Salesforce update, or the percentage of records updated within the approved period.
- **Workflow adherence:** Percentage of applicable required workflow steps completed.
- **Customer-interaction documentation:** Number or percentage of eligible customer interactions documented in Salesforce.
- **Platform activity:** Number of approved Salesforce activities or record updates.
- **Meaningful Salesforce adoption:** A possible composite of completeness, timeliness, workflow adherence, and interaction documentation.

#### Control Variables

Potential control variables may include:

- User role;
- Region or territory;
- Tenure at CVRx;
- Workload or opportunity volume;
- Baseline Salesforce adoption;
- Prior CRM experience; and
- Calendar period.

The final definitions and calculation rules will be confirmed after CVRx provides the approved Salesforce data.

### Analytics Methods to Employ

#### AO1 — Measure Meaningful Salesforce Adoption (Luis Berumen)

**Method**

AO1 will use composite-index construction and descriptive comparative analysis with approved, de-identified Salesforce records. A monthly Salesforce Adoption Index will be created for each eligible field user. The proposed index will combine five measures: opportunity update timeliness, record completeness, customer-interaction documentation, workflow consistency, and platform activity. Each measure will first be calculated and reviewed separately before the measures are combined into one score from 0 to 100.

The preliminary weights are 30% for update timeliness, 30% for record completeness, 20% for interaction documentation, 15% for workflow consistency, and 5% for platform activity. Timeliness and completeness receive the most weight because current and complete information is important for business decisions. Platform activity receives the least weight because logging in or creating activity does not always mean that Salesforce is being used effectively. These weights are proposed and will be reviewed after CVRx confirms the required fields, workflows, actions, and available data.

Each component will be calculated as a percentage of eligible work. For example, update timeliness will be based on the percentage of eligible opportunities updated within the approved timeframe, while completeness will be based on the percentage of applicable required fields containing valid information. Interaction documentation will measure the percentage of eligible accounts or opportunities with a qualifying documented interaction. Workflow consistency will measure the percentage of required steps completed when due, and platform activity will measure eligible work periods with both access and at least one meaningful action.

The analysis will summarize the overall index and each component using counts, means, medians, ranges, and distributions. Results may be compared across approved roles, territories, and time periods. Trend charts and group-comparison charts will be used to show where adoption is consistent and where records or workflows may need attention. These comparisons will be descriptive and will not be treated as evidence that a role, territory, or manager caused an adoption difference.

**Justification**

This method supports AO1 because meaningful Salesforce adoption involves more than login frequency. The index combines whether users keep information current, complete required records, document customer interactions, and follow the workflows connected to their work. Reporting each component with the overall score will prevent one combined number from hiding a specific problem.

The method also follows research that defines system usage through the relationship among the user, the system, and the task [@burtonjones2006]. This supports measuring required Salesforce work instead of treating every login or action as equally meaningful. Separating platform activity from record and information quality is also consistent with the Information Systems Success Model [@delone2003].

The user-month is the proposed unit of analysis because it allows the team to examine changes over time without relying on a single snapshot. Users will be compared with others who have similar responsibilities, and the measures will account for eligible work volume. A user with fewer active opportunities should not receive a lower score simply because there was less work to enter.

Missing information will be separated from work that was not required. If a component does not apply to a user-month, the remaining weights will be rescaled rather than assigning a zero. If a required component is unavailable because the data were not provided, the score will be marked as incomplete and will not be compared as if it were fully observed. Low, moderate, and high adoption categories will not be finalized until the baseline distribution is reviewed. Any comparison with an external industry benchmark will only be made when the benchmark uses a similar population, definition, and measurement period.

**Variables**

The primary outcome will be the Salesforce Adoption Index, calculated as:

**Salesforce Adoption Index = (Update Timeliness × .30) + (Record Completeness × .30) + (Interaction Documentation × .20) + (Workflow Consistency × .15) + (Platform Activity × .05).**

The five component scores will also be treated as separate outcomes. Comparison variables may include user role, territory or region, team, tenure, workload or opportunity volume, and calendar period when those fields are available and approved. The final calculation rules, time windows, and eligibility requirements will be confirmed with CVRx after the approved dataset is reviewed.

The five component percentages will be continuous ratio-scale measures because they have a meaningful zero and are calculated from eligible records or tasks. The overall 0-to-100 score will be treated as a continuous composite index. User role, territory, region, and team will be nominal grouping variables. Tenure and workload will be ratio-scale control variables when recorded as numerical amounts, and calendar period will be used as an ordered time variable. Because AO1 is intended to establish a baseline, the index and component scores will serve as the dependent or outcome measures rather than evidence of a causal relationship.

#### AO2 — Identify Drivers and Barriers of Meaningful Salesforce Adoption (Mickyas Shawel)

**Method**

The Salesforce data will be used to examine structural and organizational factors associated with adoption that do not depend on survey responses. A multiple regression will estimate how the Salesforce Adoption Index varies with role, region, tenure, workload and opportunity volume, using one observation per user over the baseline period.

If CVRx provides a manager or supervisor identifier, the analysis will also examine whether adoption is clustered within managers' teams. This tests the faculty lead's observation that lower adoption may be concentrated under newer supervisors. The share of variation in adoption explained by team membership will be estimated with an intraclass correlation. If clustering is substantial, models will use standard errors clustered by manager or a multilevel model with users nested within managers. Manager tenure will be added as a predictor if it is available.

If CVRx approves linking survey and Salesforce records, the survey constructs described in the Survey Data section will be added to these models. This would allow the analysis to test whether perceptions such as perceived usefulness and administrative burden remain associated with observed adoption after accounting for structural factors.

**Justification**

Some drivers of adoption are organizational rather than attitudinal. Workload, role requirements and team leadership can shape how consistently users keep Salesforce current, regardless of their individual perceptions. Salesforce records allow these factors to be measured objectively for every user, including users who do not respond to the survey. This approach reflects the organizational constructs in the Chapter 2 framework, particularly manager support and social influence (Venkatesh et al., 2003). It also provides a check on the survey findings because the outcome is observed behavior rather than self-report.

**Variables**

- **Dependent:** the Salesforce Adoption Index (SF1) and selected components.
- **Independent:** role, region, tenure group, workload or opportunity volume, and manager identifier and manager tenure if available.
- **Linked survey variables:** the seven adoption constructs (Q2–Q24), if linkage is approved.
- **Control:** calendar period and baseline adoption.

#### AO3 — Salesforce User Segmentation and Targeted Engagement (Tim Arana)

**Method**

AO3 will use a hybrid behavioral segmentation approach to identify groups of CVRx Salesforce users with similar adoption patterns. The analysis will primarily use approved, de-identified Salesforce CRM records and the meaningful adoption measures developed under AO1. The objective is to determine whether distinct groups of users demonstrate different patterns of Salesforce engagement and whether those differences can inform targeted support strategies.

The analysis will begin by examining the distribution, completeness, and comparability of relevant Salesforce activity measures. Descriptive statistics will be used to summarize adoption behaviors across users and identify potential differences in record completeness, update timeliness, interaction documentation, workflow consistency, and platform activity. Differences in role-specific responsibilities and workloads will be considered to avoid treating lower activity as evidence of weaker adoption when fewer activities are required.

If the available sample size and data quality support statistical clustering, hierarchical clustering or K-means clustering may be explored. Variables will be standardized where appropriate to prevent differences in measurement scales from disproportionately influencing the results. Candidate clustering solutions will be evaluated for stability, interpretability, and practical usefulness.

If clustering is not appropriate due to limited sample size, missing information, or insufficient variation, rule-based segmentation will be used instead. This method will classify users according to documented adoption patterns and clearly defined thresholds. The resulting groups will then be profiled using approved organizational characteristics and relevant findings from AO2.

**Justification**

Hybrid behavioral segmentation is appropriate for AO3 because Salesforce users may demonstrate different adoption behaviors and experience different challenges when using the platform. Identifying these differences can help CVRx move beyond a single engagement strategy for its entire commercial field organization.

Cluster analysis may reveal behavioral patterns that would not be apparent through predefined categories. However, statistical clustering may produce unstable or difficult-to-interpret groups when the dataset is small or contains limited behavioral variation. Rule-based segmentation provides a more transparent alternative that can be implemented consistently when clustering is not suitable.

This approach is consistent with the research framework established in Chapter 2, which emphasizes combining observed technology usage with adoption-related factors to better understand differences among users.

The resulting segments will help CVRx identify groups that may benefit from different forms of training, communication, managerial support, or workflow assistance. These recommendations will inform the targeted engagement intervention developed and evaluated under AO4.

**Variables**

The primary segmentation variables will include opportunity update timeliness, record completeness, customer interaction documentation, workflow consistency, and platform activity. These measures will be derived from the approved Salesforce records and the adoption measurement framework developed under AO1.

The overall Salesforce Adoption Index may also be examined when interpreting the resulting segments. However, overlapping measures will be evaluated to avoid assigning excessive influence to the same adoption characteristics during clustering.

Additional profiling variables may include employee role, team, territory, tenure, and other approved organizational characteristics. Where authorized, survey measures from AO2 describing perceived usefulness, training effectiveness, manager support, workflow compatibility, and administrative burden may also be incorporated to interpret differences between segments.

The final selection of variables and segmentation methods will depend on the quality, completeness, and availability of the approved Salesforce dataset.

#### AO4 — Implement and Evaluate an Engagement Campaign (Wenting Jiang)

**Method Used**

AO4 will use a longitudinal pre/post design to evaluate changes in Salesforce adoption, data quality and workflow behavior after the targeted engagement intervention. The preferred analytical method will depend on whether a credible comparison group is available.

If both an intervention group and a comparison group are available, difference-in-differences analysis will compare the baseline-to-follow-up change in the intervention group with the corresponding change in the comparison group. The interaction between intervention-group status and the post-intervention period will represent the primary estimate of intervention effectiveness.

If a comparison group is unavailable, a single-group pre/post analysis will be used. When the same users appear in both periods, paired-samples tests or their nonparametric alternatives will compare user-level outcomes. The analysis will report baseline and follow-up values, absolute and percentage changes, effect sizes and confidence intervals.

Regression models may be used to control for relevant differences in role, region, workload, opportunity volume and baseline adoption. The final model type will depend on whether the outcome is continuous, proportional, binary or a count.

**Justification for the Method**

A longitudinal design is appropriate because AO4 seeks to determine whether Salesforce behavior changes following the intervention. Existing research suggests that training, user support and workflow integration may influence sales-technology adoption and that adoption patterns can change over time.

A comparison group and difference-in-differences design are preferred because a simple pre/post change could result from seasonality, policy changes, workload changes or other organizational events. If no comparison group is available, the results will be described as changes observed after the intervention rather than definitive causal effects.

Salesforce adoption will not be evaluated through login frequency alone. The analysis will emphasize task-relevant measures such as record completeness, update timeliness, customer-interaction documentation and workflow adherence. Survey results from Section 3.1.7 will be used to help explain why behavioral changes did or did not occur.

**Variables**

The principal outcomes will include record completeness, update timeliness, workflow adherence, customer-interaction documentation and platform activity. A meaningful-adoption composite may also be considered if its scoring rules can be justified.

The primary explanatory variables will be intervention-group status, baseline versus post-intervention period, the Intervention × Post interaction and intervention exposure. Potential control variables will include role, region, tenure, workload, opportunity volume and baseline adoption. All final definitions and analytical periods will be confirmed after CVRx provides the approved data.
